This is the second part of the guide to CAS Monograph 16, *From GLMs to
Comprehensive Insurance Pricing: Techniques and Challenges*. The authors are
Chalk, Deacon, Guillen and Martinelli (2025). It is the R twin of the Python guide
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.md`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.md).
The first part,
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.qmd`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.qmd),
covers chapters 3 to 6 (measuring performance, penalized regression, nonlinear
effects, high cardinality factors). It also tells which examples the guide
reproduces, where the data comes from and how the numbers are checked. This
part covers chapters 7 to 10. The explanations are in new words, the numbers
are calculated again, and table and section numbers are the monograph's.

CI runs every R chunk that has a text block after it
(`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`). The chunk must print exactly the text of
the Python guide. The data are the same draws (read from
`examples/data/`), and the models run on the same Rust code. The boosting model
uses the same LightGBM with the same parameters.

The chunk below rebuilds, in one step, what part 1 built and this part uses:

- the simulated portfolio with its known truth (20,000 policies, folds from the
  policy number, folds 7 to 9 for testing),
- the pseudo-R2 helper and the cross-validation loop,
- the baseline GLM and boosting formulas,
- the age steps that the lasso keeps,
- the out-of-fold target encoding of make (`target_encode()`), with
  `encode_target()` for rows outside the training folds.

Part 1 explains each piece.

```{r}
library(prospicio)

# The data files, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "examples", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}

pf <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_portfolio.csv"), comment.char = "#")
toys <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_toys.csv"), comment.char = "#")
n <- nrow(pf)
pf$region <- factor(pf$region, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"))
pf$power <- factor(pf$power, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
make_effect <- toys$y[toys$example == "make_effect"]
region_effect <- c(A = 0, B = 0.15, C = -0.2, D = 0, E = 0, F = 0.3)
true_lp <- with(pf, log(0.25) + 0.9 * exp(-(age - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(age - 60, 0)^1.5 -
  0.08 * pmin(veh_age, 6) + unname(region_effect[as.character(region)]) + make_effect[make + 1] +
  0.25 * (power == "high") + 0.6 * (power == "high" & age < 25))
pf$fold <- (seq_len(n) - 1) %% 10
train <- pf$fold < 7
truth <- exp(true_lp) * pf$exposure

pseudo_r2 <- function(y, mu, expo) {
  null <- expo * sum(y) / sum(expo)
  1 - family_deviance("poisson", y, mu) / family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
}

# Python's list of formatted numbers: ['0.100', '0.200'].
py_list <- function(x, digits) {
  paste0("[", paste0("'", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x), "'", collapse = ", "), "]")
}

# Trees see region and power as the codes of their levels in alphabetical order.
tree_codes <- function(d) {
  d$region_code <- match(as.character(d$region), c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F")) - 1
  d$power_code <- match(as.character(d$power), c("high", "low", "mid")) - 1
  d
}
pf <- tree_codes(pf)
f_base <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region + power + offset(log(exposure))
f_tree <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + make + noise + offset(log(exposure))
gbm_params <- list(num_leaves = 7, min_data_in_leaf = 200, num_threads = 1)

gbm_fit <- function(formula, d, rounds = 150) {
  booster_fit(formula, d, n_rounds = rounds, learning_rate = 0.05, params = gbm_params, seed = 1)
}

cells <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ age + fold, pf, sum)
cells <- cells[order(cells$age * 10 + cells$fold), ]
knots <- seq(20, 77, by = 3)
step_names <- paste0("age_stp_", knots)
for (a in knots) cells[[paste0("age_stp_", a)]] <- as.numeric(cells$age >= a)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_steps <- reformulate(c(step_names, "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 25, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
cvp <- elastic_net_cv(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
kept <- knots[cvp$fit@coefficients[step_names, which(lams == cvp$lambda_min)] != 0]

expected <- numeric(n)
for (j in 0:6) {
  fit_j <- glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != j, ])
  expected[pf$fold == j] <- predict(fit_j, pf[pf$fold == j, ])
}
expected[!train] <- predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ])

make_level <- as.character(pf$make)

# Per policy, the log of the make's shrunk actual-to-expected ratio: a training row in fold j is
# encoded from the training folds other than j (and other than the held-out fold), every other row
# from all training folds but the held-out one.
make_feature <- function(K, held_out = -1) {
  src <- which(train & pf$fold != held_out)
  splits <- lapply(setdiff(0:6, held_out), function(j) {
    list(train = which(pf$fold[src] != j), test = which(pf$fold[src] == j))
  })
  enc <- target_encode(make_level[src], pf$claims[src], expected[src], splits, K, pf$exposure[src])
  te <- encode_target(enc$encoding, make_level)
  te[src] <- enc$rows
  log(te)
}

cat(sprintf("%d policies, %.0f claims; age steps kept by the lasso at [%s]\n",
            n, sum(pf$claims), paste(kept, collapse = ", ")))
```

```text
20000 policies, 3659 claims; age steps kept by the lasso at [20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 62, 65, 77]
```

## 1. Highly correlated variables (chapter 7)

When two features carry almost the same information, a GLM can split their
joint effect between them in many ways that fit almost equally well. Thus
small changes in the data cause large changes in the coefficients (section
7.2). The portfolio's `exper` is driver age less 17 less a small random amount.
It has a correlation of 0.997 with age and no effect of its own. The chunk
fits age and experience together on each of the seven cross-validation training
sets. It shows the changes, and what ridge and the lasso do with them (section
7.4):

```{r}
f_corr <- claims ~ age + exper + offset(log(exposure))
fits_by <- list(
  GLM = function(d) coef(glm_fit(f_corr, d)),
  ridge = function(d) elastic_net_fit(f_corr, d, alpha = 0, lambda = 0.01)@coefficients[, 1],
  lasso = function(d) elastic_net_fit(f_corr, d, alpha = 1, lambda = 0.001)@coefficients[, 1]
)
for (name in names(fits_by)) {
  coefs <- t(vapply(0:6, function(k) fits_by[[name]](pf[train & pf$fold != k, ])[c("age", "exper")],
                    double(2)))
  cat(sprintf("%-5s age %+.4f to %+.4f   exper %+.4f to %+.4f   sum %+.4f\n", name,
              min(coefs[, 1]), max(coefs[, 1]), min(coefs[, 2]), max(coefs[, 2]), mean(rowSums(coefs))))
}
```

```text
GLM   age -0.0540 to -0.0409   exper +0.0340 to +0.0467   sum -0.0072
ridge age -0.0061 to -0.0052   exper -0.0016 to -0.0010   sum -0.0070
lasso age -0.0074 to -0.0066   exper +0.0000 to +0.0000   sum -0.0070
```

The unpenalized coefficients change much from one training set to the next.
Their sum, the effect of one year of age and experience together, almost does
not change. Ridge shares the effect between the two features and keeps both
stable. The lasso keeps mostly one feature and removes the other. This is
stable here, but it can flip between training sets when the two features are
even closer (section 7.5.3).

To use principal components (section 7.4.5), calculate them with
`stats::prcomp()` on the scaled columns. Then put the components into a
formula like any other column.

## 2. Modelling in two stages (chapter 8)

### 2.1 The marketing discount as an offset

The example of chapter 8 is the only fully specified data set in the monograph.
It has one million simulated private auto policies, one year each. Age group
(A to E) and no-claims bonus (NCB 0 to 4) are strongly related. Table 8.2
prints the number of policies in each cell, and Table 8.3 prints the true
relativities. Section 8.1 gives a base frequency of 10% for age A and NCB 0. A
Poisson GLM on the 25 cells, with expected claims as the response, gives the
fit that the simulation of the monograph estimates with noise:

```{r}
table_8_2 <- list(A = c(132381, 54519, 12194, 1237, 26), B = c(55624, 82213, 49354, 12283, 952),
                  C = c(11053, 49903, 77029, 50248, 11291), D = c(920, 12187, 49027, 81946, 55690),
                  E = c(22, 1178, 12396, 54286, 132041))
age_rel <- c(A = 1, B = 0.7, C = 0.6, D = 0.5, E = 0.4)
ncb_rel <- c(1, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8)
marketing <- c(1, 0.65, 0.50, 0.40, 0.20)
data_8 <- data.frame(age = rep(names(table_8_2), each = 5), ncb = rep(0:4, 5),
                     policies = unlist(table_8_2, use.names = FALSE))
data_8$expected_claims <- data_8$policies * 0.10 * age_rel[data_8$age] * ncb_rel[data_8$ncb + 1]
data_8$mkt <- marketing[data_8$ncb + 1]
data_8$ncb <- factor(data_8$ncb)
cat(sprintf("policies %s\n", formatC(sum(data_8$policies), format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")))

full <- glm_fit(expected_claims ~ age + ncb + offset(log(policies)), data_8)
cat("age and NCB fitted:", py_list(exp(coef(full)), 3), "\n")
offset_fit <- glm_fit(expected_claims ~ age + offset(log(policies * mkt)), data_8)
rel <- unname(exp(coef(offset_fit)))
cat(sprintf("NCB offset at the marketing scale: intercept %.4f (printed 0.112)\n", rel[1]))
cat("  age B to E:", py_list(rel[-1], 4), "printed [0.849, 0.925, 0.980, 1.057]\n")
```

```text
policies 1,000,000
age and NCB fitted: ['0.100', '0.700', '0.600', '0.500', '0.400', '0.950', '0.900', '0.850', '0.800']
NCB offset at the marketing scale: intercept 0.1125 (printed 0.112)
  age B to E: ['0.8485', '0.9175', '0.9825', '1.0586'] printed [0.849, 0.925, 0.980, 1.057]
```

With age and NCB both in the model, the GLM gives the truth: intercept 0.10,
then the age and NCB relativities of Table 8.3. The monograph fit on its noisy
simulation (Table 8.4) is within about 0.025 of it. The next fit uses the NCB
scale of the marketing department as an offset and fits age again. It gives
the intercept 0.112 that section 8.1 prints (0.1125, printed as 0.112). It gives age relativities of
0.849, 0.918, 0.983 and 1.059, against the printed 0.849, 0.925, 0.980 and
1.057.

The differences come from the simulation noise of the monograph. The reversal
is the same: age relativities increase with age, because age now carries part
of the NCB effect that the marketing scale removed.

The section then gives risk premiums at a claim size of 10,000:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("true A/0 %.0f, true E/4 %.0f (printed 1,000 and 320)\n", 0.10 * 1 * 1 * 10000,
            0.10 * 0.4 * 0.8 * 10000))
cat(sprintf("GLM E/4 at printed coefficients %.0f (printed 322)\n", 0.10 * 0.39 * 0.826 * 10000))
cat(sprintf("GLM age with marketing NCB %.0f (printed 78)\n", 0.10 * 0.39 * 0.20 * 10000))
cat(sprintf("offset model E/4: printed coefficients %.0f (printed 237), recomputed %.0f\n",
            0.112 * 1.057 * 0.20 * 10000, rel[1] * rel[5] * 0.20 * 10000))
```

```text
true A/0 1000, true E/4 320 (printed 1,000 and 320)
GLM E/4 at printed coefficients 322 (printed 322)
GLM age with marketing NCB 78 (printed 78)
offset model E/4: printed coefficients 237 (printed 237), recomputed 238
```

### 2.2 Offsets and residuals give the same second stage

A second-stage model can continue from a first stage in two ways (sections 8.3
to 8.5):

- an offset of the log of the predicted counts from the first stage,
- the residual (actual over predicted counts) as the response, with the
  predicted counts as weights.

Yan and others, and Shi, show that the two are identical for a Poisson log-link
model. The chunk uses the portfolio with a first-stage GLM without region and
a second stage that fits only region:

```{r}
tr <- pf[train, ]
tr$mu1 <- predict(glm_fit(claims ~ age + veh_age + power + offset(log(exposure)), tr), tr)
by_offset <- glm_fit(claims ~ region + offset(log(mu1)), tr)
by_residual <- glm_fit(I(claims / mu1) ~ region, tr, weights = tr$mu1)
cat("offset:  ", py_list(exp(coef(by_offset)), 4), "\n")
cat("residual:", py_list(exp(coef(by_residual)), 4), "\n")
```

```text
offset:   ['0.9301', '1.2148', '0.8598', '1.0619', '1.0436', '1.4061']
residual: ['0.9301', '1.2148', '0.8598', '1.0619', '1.0436', '1.4061']
```

The two second stages are the same to the printed digits. In the summary by zip
code of section 8.4, the first rows have residuals 0 / 0.014 = 0 and
1 / 0.739 = 1.353.

Section 8.9.1 adds a caution: cross-fit the first-stage predictions, as part 1
did for `expected` in section 4.4. In a cross-fit, a model that did not see a
record predicts it. An overfitted first stage leaves nothing for the second
stage to find (Table 8.12). Cross-fitted predictions leave residuals such as
3 / 5 = 0.6 and 7 / 5 = 1.4 (Table 8.13).

For a spatial second stage like Figure 8.2, use a `gam_fit()` with the tensor
product smooth `tensors = list(c("lon", "lat"))` and the first stage as
offset.

### 2.3 Combining tables and area groups

Section 8.7 multiplies the seven aircraft tables into one relativity for the
Cessna 172M. Section 8.9.2 replaces 30,000 zip code relativities by 100 area
groups, in equal multiplicative steps between the smallest (0.379) and the
largest (1.851) relativity:

```{r}
table_8_11 <- c(1.30, 1.15, 1.00, 1.36, 1.69, 1.00, 0.41, 0.97)
cat(sprintf("Cessna 172M relativity %.2f (printed 1.37)\n", prod(table_8_11)))
step <- (1.851 / 0.379)^(1 / 99)
cat(sprintf("range %.3f (printed 4.884), exact step %.5f, printed step 1.0162, 1.0162^99 = %.3f (printed 4.908)\n",
            1.851 / 0.379, step, 1.0162^99))
cat("groups 1, 2, 3, 22, 56:", py_list(0.379 * 1.0162^(c(1, 2, 3, 22, 56) - 1), 3),
    "printed [0.379, 0.385, 0.391, 0.531, 0.917]\n")
```

```text
Cessna 172M relativity 1.37 (printed 1.37)
range 4.884 (printed 4.884), exact step 1.01615, printed step 1.0162, 1.0162^99 = 4.908 (printed 4.908)
groups 1, 2, 3, 22, 56: ['0.379', '0.385', '0.391', '0.531', '0.917'] printed [0.379, 0.385, 0.391, 0.531, 0.917]
```

The printed step 1.0162 is the exact 1.01615 rounded up. Thus 99 steps of it go
past the range (4.908 against 4.884). The monograph builds the group
relativities of Table 8.15 from the rounded step.

## 3. Learning from black-box models (chapter 9)

### 3.1 The boosting model's variance

The monograph calls the gradient boosting benchmark a very complicated GLM,
with thousands of steps and interactions. Its training performance continues to
increase as you add trees, but its validation performance stops increasing
(Figure 9.1). The chunk shows this on fold 0 of the portfolio:

```{r}
fit_d <- pf[train & pf$fold != 0, ]
val_d <- pf[pf$fold == 0, ]
for (rounds in c(50, 150, 600)) {
  b_fit <- gbm_fit(f_tree, fit_d, rounds)
  gap_train <- pseudo_r2(fit_d$claims, predict(b_fit, fit_d), fit_d$exposure)
  gap_val <- pseudo_r2(val_d$claims, predict(b_fit, val_d), val_d$exposure)
  cat(sprintf("%4d trees: train %.3f, validation %.3f\n", rounds, gap_train, gap_val))
}
```

```text
  50 trees: train 0.044, validation 0.042
 150 trees: train 0.067, validation 0.052
 600 trees: train 0.109, validation 0.051
```

### 3.2 Permutation feature importance

Section 9.2 measures the importance of a feature by how much worse the model
predicts held-out data when you shuffle the column of that feature. The shuffle
breaks the link between the feature and the outcome, and keeps everything else
the same. The method needs only predictions, so it works for any model. Tables
9.1 to 9.4 use three insureds, frequency age / 100, a model that has learned
exactly that, and the mean absolute error:

```{r}
toy_age <- c(20, 30, 40)
toy_height <- c(1.4, 1.5, 1.6)
toy_freq <- toy_age / 100
toy_model <- function(a, h) a / 100

base_mae <- mean(abs(toy_model(toy_age, toy_height) - toy_freq))
mae_age <- mean(abs(toy_model(c(40, 20, 30), toy_height) - toy_freq))
mae_height <- mean(abs(toy_model(toy_age, c(1.6, 1.4, 1.5)) - toy_freq))
gains <- c(age = mae_age - base_mae, height = mae_height - base_mae)
for (name in names(gains)) {
  cat(sprintf("%-6s increase in MAE %.3f, importance %.0f\n", name, gains[[name]],
              100 * gains[[name]] / max(gains)))
}
cat("printed: age 0.133 and 100, height 0 and 0\n")
```

```text
age    increase in MAE 0.133, importance 100
height increase in MAE 0.000, importance 0
printed: age 0.133 and 100, height 0 and 0
```

On the portfolio, "our GLM" for this chapter is the end point of the
monograph. It has the age steps that the lasso kept, steps for vehicle age,
region, power and the make encoding (at `K` = 64). It does not have the noise
and experience features (part 1, sections 3.2 and 4.4).

The boosting model gets the raw features and the same make encoding, as in the
monograph. The monograph notes that the two models would share one encoding if
its boosting library did not have a built-in encoding. The boosting model does
not get `exper`, because this near-copy of age would blur every comparison
below. This is the caveat of section 9.2 about correlated features.

As in section 9.5.1, each importance is the average over the seven
cross-validation models, each on its held-out fold. The importance is the loss
of pseudo-R2 when the feature is shuffled. `permutation_importance()` takes a score to minimize, so
the pseudo-R2 goes in with a negative sign.

The `splits` argument of `permutation_importance()` can fit the models itself. But here the make
encoding changes for each held-out fold. Thus the loop fits the two models on
each fold and explains them on the held-out rows of that fold. The fold number
is the seed of the shuffle. Then the loop calculates the average of the seven results. The same loop also runs what the next
two sections need: `partial_dependence()` on age and the pairwise `interaction_screen()`. The shuffles come from prospicio's `permutation()`, so
the shuffles and the numbers equal those of the Python guide.

```{r}
veh_knots <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
features <- c("age", "veh_age", "region", "power", "log_te", "noise")
ages <- c(18, 21, 25, 40, 60, 75)

# The formula builds the step columns and the interaction from the frame's own columns, so
# predict() rebuilds them on whatever frame the helpers pass (shuffled, or with age set to one value).
glm_formula <- function(interaction = FALSE) {
  reformulate(c(sprintf("I(as.numeric(age >= %d))", kept), sprintf("I(as.numeric(veh_age >= %d))", veh_knots),
                "region", "power", "log_te", if (interaction) "I(as.numeric(age < 25 & power == 'high'))",
                "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
}
f_gbm <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + log_te + noise + offset(log(exposure))

frame <- function(mask, log_te) {
  f <- pf[mask, c("age", "veh_age", "region", "power", "region_code", "power_code", "noise", "exposure",
                  "claims")]
  f$log_te <- log_te[mask]
  f
}

# Region and power are shuffled together with the trees' codes for them.
groups <- list(age = "age", veh_age = "veh_age", region = c("region", "region_code"),
               power = c("power", "power_code"), log_te = "log_te", noise = "noise")
neg_r2 <- function(model, f) -pseudo_r2(f$claims, predict(model, f), f$exposure)
fit_model <- list(GLM = function(f) glm_fit(glm_formula(), f), GBM = function(f) gbm_fit(f_gbm, f))
imp_by <- list(GLM = list(), GBM = list())
pd_by <- list(GLM = list(), GBM = list())
screen_by <- list()
glm_with_interaction <- numeric()
for (k in 0:6) {
  log_te_k <- make_feature(64, held_out = k)
  fit_f <- frame(train & pf$fold != k, log_te_k)
  val_f <- frame(pf$fold == k, log_te_k)
  for (m in c("GLM", "GBM")) {
    model <- fit_model[[m]](fit_f)
    imp_by[[m]][[k + 1]] <- permutation_importance(model, val_f, neg_r2, groups, seed = k)
    pd_by[[m]][[k + 1]] <- partial_dependence(model, val_f, "age", ages)$mean
    if (m == "GBM") screen_by[[k + 1]] <- interaction_screen(model, val_f, neg_r2, groups, seed = k)
  }
  with_i <- glm_fit(glm_formula(TRUE), fit_f)
  glm_with_interaction <- c(glm_with_interaction,
                            pseudo_r2(val_f$claims, predict(with_i, val_f), val_f$exposure))
}

score_full <- lapply(imp_by, function(v) -mean(vapply(v, attr, double(1), "base")))
mean_loss <- lapply(imp_by, function(v) {
  setNames(rowMeans(sapply(v, function(imp) imp$importance)), v[[1]]$feature)
})
cat(sprintf("cv pseudo-R2: GLM %.3f, GBM %.3f\n", score_full$GLM, score_full$GBM))
cat(sprintf("%-8s %9s %9s\n", "feature", "GLM loss", "GBM loss"))
for (x in features[order(-mean_loss$GLM[features])]) {
  cat(sprintf("%-8s %9.3f %9.3f\n", x, mean_loss$GLM[[x]], mean_loss$GBM[[x]]))
}
```

```text
cv pseudo-R2: GLM 0.055, GBM 0.048
feature   GLM loss  GBM loss
log_te       0.039     0.033
age          0.037     0.034
power        0.019     0.019
veh_age      0.011     0.009
region       0.008     0.003
noise        0.000    -0.000
```

The two models agree on which features are important and approximately on their
order. The GBM gives the noise feature almost no importance, although it can
use it. With the monograph's treatment of nonlinear effects and of make, our
GLM now scores above this untuned boosting model. In section 1.3 of part 1, the
raw-feature baseline GLM was far below it.

The GLM loss for noise is exactly zero because the GLM does not use noise. The
GLM importances in the monograph are never exactly zero, because its lasso kept
each feature in at least one fold.

### 3.3 Partial dependence

Section 9.3 isolates the effect of a feature in a black box. It sets the
feature to one value for every record, calculates the average prediction, and
repeats for another value. For a GLM without interactions, the ratio of the two
averages is exactly the ratio of the relativities of the feature. The printed
`nu_registered` steps give 1.107 between 1 and 10. Tables 9.7 to 9.9 give the
same ratio from predictions, and the boosting model of Table 9.10 gives 1.104:

```{r}
nu <- function(v) -0.0001407 * v + 0.02936 * (v >= 2) + 0.07342 * (v >= 7) - 0.15822 * (v >= 16) -
  0.17117 * (v >= 35)
cat(sprintf("GLM relativity 10 vs 1 from the steps %.3f (printed 1.107)\n", exp(nu(10) - nu(1))))
cat(sprintf("Table 9.9 ratio of totals %.3f, Table 9.10 GBM %.3f (printed 1.107, 1.104)\n",
            0.01225 / 0.01107, 0.005892 / 0.005336))
```

```text
GLM relativity 10 vs 1 from the steps 1.107 (printed 1.107)
Table 9.9 ratio of totals 1.107, Table 9.10 GBM 1.104 (printed 1.107, 1.104)
```

On the portfolio, the chunk shows the partial dependence of each model on
driver age. Each value is relative to age 40 and averaged over the seven
held-out folds. The
truth for a low-power car is next to it. The true young-driver effect is larger
for high power, which is the interaction:

```{r}
true_age <- exp(0.9 * exp(-(ages - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(ages - 60, 0)^1.5)
pd_mean <- lapply(pd_by, function(v) colMeans(do.call(rbind, v)))
for (i in seq_along(ages)) {
  cat(sprintf("age %d: GLM %.2f  GBM %.2f  true (low power) %.2f\n", ages[i],
              pd_mean$GLM[i] / pd_mean$GLM[4], pd_mean$GBM[i] / pd_mean$GBM[4], true_age[i] / true_age[4]))
}
```

```text
age 18: GLM 2.81  GBM 2.39  true (low power) 2.40
age 21: GLM 2.06  GBM 1.85  true (low power) 1.69
age 25: GLM 1.54  GBM 1.18  true (low power) 1.29
age 40: GLM 1.00  GBM 1.00  true (low power) 1.00
age 60: GLM 1.00  GBM 1.02  true (low power) 0.98
age 75: GLM 1.18  GBM 1.09  true (low power) 1.07
```

Section 9.3 gives a caution: a partial dependence is an average over the
portfolio. The young-driver figures of both models mix high-power cars, where
the effect is stronger, with the other cars. The GLM figure is higher. Without
an interaction term, the GLM charges every young driver part of the extra load
of high-power cars. The next section finds that interaction.

### 3.4 Interactions from permutations

The interaction screen of section 9.4 shuffles two features separately and
together. Let `L_A`, `L_B` and `L_AB` be the losses. Then `L_A + L_B - L_AB` is
zero if neither feature interacts with anything. It is positive if the two
features interact with each other or with a common third feature. Table 9.11
prints the three losses for three pairs with aircraft age. From the values, its
columns are `L_AB`, `L_A` and `L_B`:

```{r}
table_9_11 <- data.frame(name = c("region", "nu_registered", "faa_eng_hp_char"),
                         l_ab = c(0.291, 0.115, 0.123), l_a = c(0.253, 0.016, 0.002),
                         l_b = c(0.135, 0.135, 0.135), printed = c("0.096", "0.037", "0.014"))
for (i in 1:3) {
  r <- table_9_11[i, ]
  cat(sprintf("%-15s x aircraft age: %.3f (printed %s)\n", r$name, r$l_a + r$l_b - r$l_ab, r$printed))
}
```

```text
region          x aircraft age: 0.097 (printed 0.096)
nu_registered   x aircraft age: 0.036 (printed 0.037)
faa_eng_hp_char x aircraft age: 0.014 (printed 0.014)
```

The recalculated values differ from the printed values by 0.001, because the
three inputs are rounded. The next chunk runs the same screen on the boosting
model, over each pair of portfolio features, averaged over the seven folds.
Then it gives the cross-validated GLM score with and without one more column
for the first pair:

```{r}
screen <- screen_by[[1]][c("a", "b")]
screen$strength <- rowMeans(sapply(screen_by, function(s) s$strength))
screen <- screen[order(-screen$strength), ]
for (i in 1:3) cat(sprintf("%-8s x %-8s %.4f\n", screen$a[i], screen$b[i], screen$strength[i]))
cat(sprintf("GLM cv pseudo-R2 %.3f, with a young-driver high-power term %.3f\n",
            score_full$GLM, mean(glm_with_interaction)))
```

```text
age      x power    0.0051
age      x log_te   0.0012
veh_age  x noise    0.0006
GLM cv pseudo-R2 0.055, with a young-driver high-power term 0.058
```

Age and power come first, which is the planted interaction, and the GLM
improves with it. The next pairs have a quarter of its strength or less, and
their order changes with the shuffle. (The third pair includes the noise
feature, which interacts with nothing.)

In the monograph, the leaves of a decision tree fitted to the ratio of boosting
to GLM predictions did this work. They increased the cross-validated pseudo-R2
from 0.151 to 0.156. a `booster_fit()` with one tree and a few leaves is a decision
tree, and the hand-made column above uses the same idea.

### 3.5 The test data, once

All decisions above used only the training folds. The rule of section 3.2 is to
look at the test data once, at the end. The chunk fits each model again on all
seven training folds, with the make encoding from all of them. Then it scores
each model on folds 7 to 9:

```{r}
log_te_all <- make_feature(64)
fit_all <- frame(train, log_te_all)
test_all <- frame(!train, log_te_all)
final <- list(
  "baseline GLM" = predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ]),
  "our GLM" = predict(glm_fit(glm_formula(), fit_all), test_all),
  "our GLM + interaction" = predict(glm_fit(glm_formula(TRUE), fit_all), test_all),
  "GBM" = predict(gbm_fit(f_gbm, fit_all), test_all),
  "truth" = truth[!train]
)
for (name in names(final)) {
  cat(sprintf("%-22s %.3f\n", name, pseudo_r2(test_all$claims, final[[name]], test_all$exposure)))
}
```

```text
baseline GLM           0.025
our GLM                0.068
our GLM + interaction  0.071
GBM                    0.064
truth                  0.089
```

The ranking on the test data is the one that cross-validation predicted. The
truth is first, then our GLM with the interaction, our GLM, the boosting model
and the baseline. The last digit of the boosting model can change with the LightGBM
version and platform. The last digits of the GLMs cannot.

## 4. Challenges in ratemaking models (chapter 10)

The last chapter lists ways that a good cross-validation score can still
mislead:

- data with a misunderstood meaning (the aircraft age of the monograph was the
  years since the registration certificate, not since manufacture),
- technical errors, such as factor levels coded differently in training and
  production (a fitted model keeps its factor levels, and `predict()` builds
  the design with them),
- data that breaks the assumptions of the model,
- coefficients and business mix that drift over time,
- regulation,
- outliers and data quality.

Cross-validation fails when the future differs from the folds, so monitor a
model in production. `actual_vs_expected()` compares actual and expected claims by period. It
gives a z-score for each period and a test for a trend in the ratio, the check
that section 10.4 asks for.
